1. **Chart type**: Scatter plot.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
- Single-panel chart  
- No faceting or small multiples  
- Uses reference lines (vertical and horizontal averages) to divide the plot into quadrants  
- No stacking

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Average yearly salary during contract | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Average yearly WAR during contract | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Player name / contract label | Categorical/nominal | Text label next to points |
| Above/below average salary threshold | Quantitative-derived grouping | Vertical dashed reference line / shaded right-side region |
| Above/below average WAR threshold | Quantitative-derived grouping | Horizontal dashed reference line / shaded lower region |

Notes:
- All points use the same color and shape, so color does not appear to encode a separate data variable.
- The shaded lower-right quadrant visually emphasizes contracts with above-average salary and below-average WAR.

comments.raw_comment:
I notice that there appears to be a correlation between a baseball player’s value, or WAR, and their average salary throughout their 10-year contract. I also notice that there appears to be a cluster in the middle such that most players are relatively close to the center point, implying that the average yearly salary of players is indicative of their WAR. 
I wonder why those who deviate from the typical range depicted in the graph do so. Some examples include Albert Pujois, who does not earn a lot (less $15,000,000) despite having the second-highest WAR, and Ryan Howard, getting paid $25,000,000 for having a negative WAR.
This graph relates to my community and me in that we can generalize these findings to demonstrate that, typically, our contribution to a team dictates our payoff. Given that it is possible that people in my current classes and social circle can end up working together with each other or with me as part of a team later down the line, it is important we each positively contribute to project efforts.
Catchy Headline: “WAR: Does Your Contract Value Your Contributions to the Team?”

comments.raw_comment:
What I notice:

The graph compares the average yearly WAR (Wins Above Replacement) and average yearly salary during 10-year MLB contracts.
There is a clear trend that players with higher average yearly WAR tend to earn higher average yearly salaries.
However, the relationship is not perfectly linear. Some players like Mike Trout stand out as having an exceptionally high WAR relative to their salary.
There also seems to be more variability in salaries at the higher end of the WAR spectrum.

What I wonder:

What other factors besides on-field performance (WAR) impact player salaries? 

Are teams getting good value from these mega long-term contracts, or do they tend to backfire as players age? Comparing salary to WAR over the full contract would be informative.

How has this relationship between WAR and salary for top contracts evolved over time as analytics and player valuations have advanced?

Impact on the sport and fanbases:

As teams commit huge sums to top stars, it could impact competitive balance, roster construction, and fan perception if highly paid players underperform.

However, building around contracted superstars allows fanbases to have long-term attachment to franchise icons.

As younger stars like Juan Soto sign massive deals, it will be fascinating to see how the market evolves and if they live up to expectations.

Potential headline: "MLB's big money bets: The relationship between star players' production and pay in an era of mega contracts"

comments.raw_comment:
When looking at this graph, I noticed several things. Many of the baseball players are clustered around the same average WAR, with an equal number of players both above and below the WAR average. However, I appears that there are more players below the WAR average than above or right along it. Additionally, a few players, such as Albert Pujols, Alex Rodriguez, and Miguel Cabrera, have more than one contract. I wonder why, for players with two contracts, such as Albert Pujols, Alex Rodriguez, and Miguel Cabrera, their WAR is higher during their first contract but drops significantly in their second contract, while their salary increases in the second contract. This may be because these players lack motivation after getting such a huge boost in salary, or even simply that just the older they get, they tend to slow down. This relates to me personally as I currently work for a college baseball team, see taking notes on more in-depth baseball statistics really intrigues me. While it may not have a great affect on my community as a whole, my personal interest and work environment leads me to enjoy this data. 

Headline: "Baseball WAR: The Battle of Performance in Relation to Salary"

   I find it very strange that people who only provide some entertainment get paid so much when they are not contributing anything very important to our community. comments.raw_comment: When I was doing research on the individuals in this graph, and I noticed that not all of the players were active at the same time. For instance, Mike Trout started playing in 2009, while Kevin Brown retired in 2006. This makes it impossible for this chart to have been, at any time, accurate to that time. This means that this chart has to have been compiled recently, but before people like Ryan Howard retired. Additionally, this graph had to have been made before March of 2019 because Mike Trout’s salary has drastically changed since this chart was created. On a different note, when I look at this chart, I break it into four pieces, the bad players with low salaries, the bad players with good salaries, good players with bad salaries, and good players with good salaries. In these four groups, I see two main categories, the fair and unfair deals, the good players with good pay and the bad players with bad pay. These sections are fair because the managers and the players get exactly the right amount for what they pay, money and labor. On the other hand, the other two categories are unfair because either the player is paid to much in which case they might be released, or the player is paid to little in which case they might quit. All in all, there is a lot to be learned from this chart, an expanse of knowledge that this comment only skims the surface of.

Honestly, I do not really follow baseball statistics, but I do watch it. I notice that on the scatter plot graph, there are a lot of people who are towards the middle, or closer to the bottom, but then there are those five or so people who are above all others, way at the top. Also, I notice how nobody really overlaps, or has the same contract. There are people who have an average salary from this array of people, and then there are also people who have an average WAR. 
I wonder why there are not any of the same contracts, and why there are lots of people around the same salary, but then there is the few people who are above the rest. Also, why do some people have a higher pay, but not for the reason of their playing? Why are players not paid by their skill level? Personally, I think that the baseball players should be paid based on their skill level, because I feel like that is the thing that matters when you are trying to get someone on your team.

It was also cool to see how teams were overplaying players, who weren’t performing up to their standards. It seems as though the Cardinals got a steal when they payed Albert Pujols for his first contact. Then, on his second contract, he got payed a lot more money, but did not perform as well as he did during his first contact. The person who seems to be getting the most overpaid and not performing is Ryan Howard. It hurts to say that being a Phillies fan, but I can see how was sort of an all or nothing guy. Based on his WAR, he doesn’t help his team more than he actually helps his team, yet he is still getting paid loads of money. Good for him, but not for his team.

comments.raw_comment: Baseball doesn't interest me, but I do find this graph fascinating. The first thing glaring out is Mike Trout's WAR to salary ratio. He is the "best" player out of everyone in the graph, but he does't get nearly as much money as Zack Greinke who has a close-to-average WAR. Furthermore, this is the same case with Albert Pujols. He has the second most WAR in his first contract, but his salary is below average. As he reaches his second contract, Pujols has a significantly lower WAR, but higher salary. Why is this the case? Finally, I see that Ryan Howard has a negative WAR number. How can someone be that bad? On top of that, how can someone that bad get a higher salary than the hardest, best player (Mike Trout)? This confuses me, but I think this shows how not everything is fair in life. Some people get granted advantages. Some people don't. If I were to name this graph, I would call it "The Cost of WAR."

comments.raw_comment: I am not interested in sports, so I barely understand this graph. In the graph, I notice that players who have lower wars are paid more, but some of the players who have higher WARs are paid less. I wonder why this is? Logically, it does not make sense. Another question that I have is if Mike Trout has the highest WAR which is between 8 and 9, how is he not paid the most? There is a similar issue other players including Alex Rodriguez and Albert Pujols. Even though they don’t have the highest WAR, they do have a large amount, so I would expect them to get paid more than they do. Another thing about this graph that stands out is that a lot of the players who have a low WAR are paid the average yearly salary or more. I don’t get this because players who have around the same WAR are paid different amounts. The amounts vary by a lot. For example, Carlos Lee and Yoenis Cespedes have about the same WAR, but one makes less than the average yearly salary. If I had to title this graph, I would name it WAR vs. salary.

comments.raw_comment: This graph has many questions circling around it. Fist off, I noticed that a lot of players had a really high WAR but a lower pay than many others. It confuses me why players aren’t paid based on ability, but what team offers the better contract. Mike Trout has the highest WAR in the whole league, but nowhere near the highest pay. I understand that teams offer a higher paying contract if the athlete has a high WAR, but abilities change. In my opinion, the MLB should pay the players based off of WAR and not luck of a team’s contract. To title this graph, I would call it The “WAR” of the Contract.

If I were to name this graph, I would call it, “WAR in Relation to Pay”.

comments.raw_comment:
Welcome to Wednesday's moderation of  “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Today’s graph compares baseball players with contracts of at least $100 Million.  It compares their annual salary with their how good they have been as measured by their WAR (Wins Above Replacement or past player wins greater than how many a rookie (new) replacement player would be expected to have).

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?",  "What do you wonder?", and  "What's going on in this graph?"  

Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas about the graph. 

On Thursday afternoon, we’ll reveal the article that included this graph and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.

The next “What’s Going On in This Graph?” will be in September.  To get next year’s schedule and the early Friday releases, register for the Learning Network Friday newsletter athttps://tinyurl.com/LNNewsletterAlso, to view the March 20 webinar about teaching with graphs from The New York Times, go tohttps://tinyurl.com/GraphWebinar.
